title: Consented Change Orchestrator - PRD (rough)
summary: Draft PRD for a Consented Change Orchestrator: a lightweight control plane feature for customer-managed networking in Private deployments that centralizes approval gates, generates compact tamper-evident audit artifacts, and offers a migration path from operator-managed approvals to customer-consented workflows.
body:
Problem statement:

Customers running Redwood Private want deterministic, auditable change workflows for network and control-plane changes (eg. VPC routing, peering, egress rules, operator sidecars). Right now we have ad-hoc operator approvals and large bulk audit bundles that are hard to query and difficult for customers to integrate into their own SIEMs. Teams also ask for a mode where the customer can explicitly grant or deny changes (consent), and for a compact, verifiable artifact to ship with every change that proves which party authorized it and why.

Objectives / Goals (MVP):
- Provide an orchestration primitive ("consent flow") that ties a requested change to a minimal, signed audit artifact and an approval result.
- Ensure artifacts are easy to ingest by customer-managed logging (syslog/forwarders) and by Redwood Console for troubleshooting.
- Support two modes: operator-assisted consent (Redwood proposes, customer consents) and self-service consent (customer triggers changes through their UI or CI).
- Keep latency minimal: consent path should not add more than 3s median to typical operator workflows when using our fast path.
- Provide a clear rollback and emergency-override story for on-call operations.

Success metrics (first 90 days):
- 80% of customer-managed VPC changes for pilot customers flow through the consented change orchestrator.
- Median time-to-approval for standard consent flows < 30s for automated (CI) flows and < 10m for manual human approval flows.
- Audit artifact ingestion success rate > 99.5% to customer syslog endpoints in pilot.
- No customer-facing incidents caused by consent artifact failures in pilot.

User personas and stories:
- Platform Engineer (customer): "I want a compact, signed record for each network change so my compliance team can verify who approved it and what changed."
- SRE (Redwood operator): "If a change is blocked by the customer, I need guidance on rollback and an immutable trace to show why we aborted."
- Security Compliance Officer (customer): "We need the audit artifacts to contain the policy evaluation result, a minimal diff, and retention metadata so we can retain for 2 years in our archive."

High-level flow (textual):
1) Change requested (operator API, customer API, or CI webhook) -> creates a Change Intent record with a short UUID and a compact diff of the proposed change.
2) Policy evaluation runs locally against the customer's policy bundle (if present) and returns an allowance score and list of checks.
3) Consent gate is triggered: a fast path (automated consent via signed customer key / CI token) or manual path (email/push/console notification to approvers).
4) Approver decision recorded; a signed Consent Token is produced. Consent Token = {change-id, approver-id, decision, timestamp, policy-hash, minimal-diff, ttl}. Token is signed by Redwood and optionally co-signed by customer's KMS public key in Private installations.
5) Execution: optimizer routes change to runtime; an immutable Audit Capsule is appended to the customer's audit stream and to Redwood's internal compact ledger.
6) Post-change verification: optional health probe and revert trigger window.

Audit artifact (compact capsule) design notes:
- Capsule is intentionally narrow to make ingestion cheap. Fields: change-id, change-summary (short text), initiator, approver(s), consent-token-hash, policy-check-summary (2–3 bullet checks), timestamp, optional co-signature, retention-tag.
- We surface a human-readable 1-line summary + compact diff (max 2KB). If diffs are bigger, store a pointer to the long-form evidence bundle (s3-like URI) and keep the capsule small.
- Capsules are signed using Redwood signing key; in Private deployments, customers can request co-signing via their KMS (asymmetric public key uploaded once).
- Capsules will be emitted to: customer syslog/forwarder, Redwood Console event stream, and an archival bucket for forensic queries.

Approval gates and policies:
- Gate types: require-consent, suggest-only, automated-allow, emergency-override.
- Policies are evaluated both server-side (Redwood runtime) and client-side (optional local policy agent in customer VPC for zero-trust customers).
- For some high-risk changes (eg. egress-to-public), default is require-consent with at least two approvers in manual mode.
- Every gate must map to a Jira ticket or incident id if triggered as part of an incident rollout.

APIs and UX sketch (surface-level):
- POST /v1/private/changes/intents -> returns change-id, preview.
- GET /v1/private/changes/intents/{id} -> status (pending | approved | denied | executed | failed).
- POST /v1/private/changes/intents/{id}/approve -> body: {approver-id, decision, comment, ttl}.
- Webhook contract: Redwood emits a compact JSON capsule to configured endpoint at final state.
- Console: a compact timeline view with the capsule hash, short diff, actor badges, and a single-click revert (if allowed).

Security & compliance considerations:
- Signing model: Redwood signs for integrity; private customers can register a public key for co-signing. We must design key rotation flows and a revocation list.
- Tamper-evidence: audit capsules include a monotonic sequence and a server-signed checkpoint (fast Merkle-ish chain) to allow efficient spot-checks without shipping the entire ledger.
- Data minimization: capsule stores only the minimal-diff; sensitive values must be redacted before capsule emission (customer redaction rules applied).
- Retention: customer-configurable retention tags; default retention 365 days for console; customers can request export and long-term retention to their storage.

Rollback & emergency paths:
- Emergency override: Redwood operator may execute with an emergency flag; this produces an Emergency Capsule that explicitly records reason, operator justification, and customer-notification timestamp. Emergency actions are gated by SLAs and must be reconciled within the next 24 hours.
- Automatic revert window: for certain change types, a time-limited auto-revert can be configured (eg. revert if health-checks fail in 10 minutes).

Data model example (human text, not JSON schema):
- Change Intent: id, requester, source (operator|customer|CI), minimal-diff, created_at, policy-hash.
- Consent Token: token-id, change-id, approver-list, decision, sig-redwood, sig-customer? , ttl, created_at.
- Audit Capsule: capsule-id, change-id, capsule-hash, short-summary, approver, policy-eval-summary, signatures, created_at, retention-tag, pointer-to-evidence.

Pilot plan and rollout:
- Phase 0 (experiments): implement capsule emitter and local policy evaluator; run internally on staging with SRE.
- Phase 1 (alpha pilots): onboard 2-3 low-risk customers with operator-assisted consent. Enable syslog forwarding and measure ingestion/latency.
- Phase 2 (beta): enable co-signing with one customer KMS; test emergency overrides and auto-revert windows.
- Phase 3 (general availability): console UI, SDKs, and operator runbook published.

Operational runbooks (brief):
- If Capsule emission fails to customer endpoint: queue to retry, mark intent as executed but flagged; alert customer via alternate channel; surface retry count in console.
- If signature verification fails on customer's side: provide a "verify key" endpoint and an ephemeral signing test to validate rotation.
- If emergency action used: create audit ticket PD-KEEP and require postmortem with timeline, capsule links, and approval justification.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Co-signing complexity: tying co-signatures to customer KMS improves trust but increases operational support burden (key rotation, on-prem HSM network constraints).
- Artifact size vs fidelity: how much diff to keep in-capsule vs long-form evidence? Defaulting to small capsules keeps telemetry cheap.
- Offline approvals: customers that operate in air-gapped environments may need a signed offline token exchange protocol. Design for this in Phase 2.

Next steps / immediate action items:
- [Avery] Draft proto capsule JSON schema and small reference emitter library (Go + Python) - due 2025-01-26.
- [Maya] Wire up syslog and S3 delivery paths for pilot customers - due 2025-02-09.
- [Samir] Spike co-signing flow with test KMS and validation flow - due 2025-02-02.
- [Lena] Write operator-runbook and emergency override acceptance criteria - due 2025-02-05.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally light on rigid schema choices; priority is to get a small shipping artifact that customers can easily consume.
- Please annotate open questions inline in Confluence page linked above and tag PD-2107 in Jira for tracking.

Appendix (examples):
- Example capsule one-liner: "capsule: cid-93f4a2 | change: add-egress-to-10.0.0.0/8 | approver: infra-team@custco | decision: approved | ts:2025-01-12T14:03Z"
- Example emergency capsule note: "EMERGENCY: forced-replace-gateway | operator: infra-oncall@redwood | reason: customer downtime > 3m | ticket:INC-7743"

End of draft.
